133: // Narrow a key record to a link, or undefined if it's an alias.
134: function asLink(record: ShareKeyRecord | undefined): ShareLinkRecord | undefined {
135:   return record !== undefined && record.alias === undefined ? record : undefined;
136: }
137: 
138: /**
139:  * Per-session caller identity. Mirrors the fields the OverseerClientInterface holds for the
140:  * connected client.
141:  */
142: export interface SharingCaller {
143:   /** The caller's profile.id (username/email). */
144:   profileId: string;
145:   /**
146:    * True if the caller is the gadget owner. The owner can manage anyone's collaborator edges
147:    * and share keys; non-owners are restricted to edges/keys they created themselves.
148:    */
149:   isOwner: boolean;
150: }
151: 
152: export class SharingManager {
153:   /**
154:    * `ownerProfileId` is stable for the lifetime of a gadget, so it's supplied once at
155:    * construction rather than per call.
156:    */
157:   constructor(private storage: SharingStorage, private ownerProfileId: string) {}
158: 
159:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
160:   // Sharing-state queries
161: 
162:   /**
163:    * True if anyone other than the owner can currently access the gadget. Used by the Overseer's
164:    * `prohibitAllSharing` policy to decide whether a sensitive observation must be blocked.
165:    *
166:    * Because removed collaborators and revoked links linger in storage (the lazy revocation model;
167:    * see the module header and removeCollaborator/revokeShareLink), this must reflect *current*
168:    * reachability, not mere table membership: a collaborator with a live path from the owner, or
169:    * an un-revoked share link whose keys anyone could still redeem.
170:    */
171:   hasAnyShares(): boolean {
172:     if (this.computeEffectiveRoles().size > 0) return true;
173:     for (let link of this.#listLinks()) {
174:       if (!link.revoked) return true;
175:     }
176:     return false;
177:   }
178: 
179:   // Every share link, revoked or not. Aliases are skipped.
180:   *#listLinks(): Generator<ShareLinkRecord> {
181:     for (let record of this.storage.shareKeys.list()) {
182:       let link = asLink(record);
183:       if (link) yield link;
184:     }
185:   }
186: 
187:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
188:   // Authorization (used by Overseer.open())
189: 
190:   /**
191:    * True if `profileId` currently has a collaborator record. This only checks membership; use
192:    * `getEffectiveRole()` to determine the actual access level (and whether the record is still
193:    * reachable from the owner in the permission graph).
194:    */
195:   isCollaborator(profileId: string): boolean {
196:     return this.storage.collaborators.get(profileId) !== undefined;
197:   }
198: 
199:   /**
200:    * The effective role of `profileId` -- the maximum role reachable from the owner through valid
201:    * permission edges -- or undefined if the user has no access. The owner always has "build".
202:    */
203:   getEffectiveRole(profileId: string): CollaboratorRole | undefined {
204:     if (profileId === this.ownerProfileId) return "build";
205:     return this.computeEffectiveRoles().get(profileId);
206:   }
207: 
208:   /**
209:    * Redeem a raw share key on behalf of a user opening the gadget. If the key exists, ensures the
210:    * user is a collaborator with a `shareKey` edge for its link (adding the edge if missing, or
211:    * creating the collaborator record if they're new). Does nothing if the key is unknown.
212:    *
213:    * The raw key is hashed internally; the plaintext is never stored. `fetchProfile` is invoked
214:    * (an RPC, in production) only when a brand-new collaborator must be created, so existing
215:    * collaborators are redeemed without any RPC.
216:    *
217:    * A key whose link is revoked behaves like an unknown key (it cannot be redeemed).
218:    */
219:   async redeemShareKey(opts: {
220:     rawKey: string;
221:     profileId: string;
222:     fetchProfile: () => Promise<AiChatAuthorInfo>;
223:   }): Promise<void> {
224:     let hash = await hashShareKey(opts.rawKey);
225:     let keyRecord = this.storage.shareKeys.get(hash);
226:     if (!keyRecord) return;
227: 
228:     // Edges point at the link, not the individual key, so a link's keys collapse to one grant.
229:     // A copy of a link is an alias; follow it to the link that owns the metadata.
230:     let link = keyRecord.alias === undefined
231:         ? keyRecord : asLink(this.storage.shareKeys.get(keyRecord.alias));
232:     if (!link || link.revoked) return;
233:     let linkId = link.id;
234:     let role = link.role ?? "build";
235: 
236:     let existing = this.storage.collaborators.get(opts.profileId);
237:     if (existing) {
238:       // User is already a collaborator. Only add an edge if they don't already have one for this
239:       // link (redeeming a second key of the same link is a no-op).
240:       let alreadyHasEdge = existing.addedBy.some(
241:           e => e.type === "shareKey" && e.keyId === linkId);
242:       if (!alreadyHasEdge) {
243:         existing.addedBy.push({
244:           type: "shareKey",
245:           keyId: linkId,
246:           created: new Date(),
247:           role,
248:         });
249:         this.storage.collaborators.put(existing);
250:       }
251:     } else {
252:       // New collaborator -- need full profile from their user DO.
253:       let profile = await opts.fetchProfile();
254:       this.storage.collaborators.put({
255:         profile,
256:         addedBy: [{
257:           type: "shareKey",
258:           keyId: linkId,
259:           created: new Date(),
260:           role,
261:         }],
262:       });
263:     }
264:   }
265: 
266:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
267:   // Collaborator management
268: 
269:   /**
270:    * List currently-active collaborators -- those with a live path from the owner. Under the lazy
271:    * revocation model, removed collaborators linger in storage with no reachable role; they are
272:    * omitted here (they reappear if re-added).
273:    */
274:   listCollaborators(): CollaboratorInfo[] {
275:     let roles = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
276:     let result: CollaboratorInfo[] = [];
277:     for (let record of this.storage.collaborators.list()) {
278:       let role = roles.get(record.profile.id);
279:       if (!role) continue;  // not currently reachable from the owner
280:       result.push({
281:         profile: record.profile,
282:         addedBy: record.addedBy,
283:         role,
284:       });
285:     }
286:     return result;
287:   }
288: 
289:   /**
290:    * Add a collaborator with a `user` edge from the caller, granting `role`. The caller is
291:    * responsible for resolving `profile` (via RPC) and for any policy checks (e.g.
292:    * `prohibitAllSharing`). The caller may not grant a role higher than their own effective role.
293:    */
294:   addCollaborator(opts: {
295:     caller: SharingCaller;
296:     profile: AiChatAuthorInfo;
297:     role: CollaboratorRole;
298:     note?: string;
299:   }): CollaboratorInfo {
300:     // Don't add the owner as a collaborator.
301:     if (opts.profile.id === this.ownerProfileId) {
302:       throw new Error("Cannot add the workspace owner as a collaborator.");
303:     }
304: 
305:     let callerRole = this.#requireCallerRole(opts.caller);
306:     if (roleRank(opts.role) > roleRank(callerRole)) {
307:       throw new Error("You cannot grant a role higher than your own.");
308:     }
309: 
310:     let existing = this.storage.collaborators.get(opts.profile.id);
311:     let edge: PermissionEdge = {
312:       type: "user",
313:       sharer: opts.caller.profileId,
314:       created: new Date(),
315:       role: opts.role,
316:       note: opts.note,
317:     };
318: 
319:     if (existing) {
320:       // Already a collaborator -- add an edge if they don't have one from this sharer, otherwise
321:       // upgrade the existing edge's role (never silently downgrade).
322:       let existingEdge = existing.addedBy.find(
323:           e => e.type === "user" && e.sharer === opts.caller.profileId);
324:       if (existingEdge && existingEdge.type === "user") {
325:         existingEdge.role = maxRole(edgeGrantedRole(existingEdge), opts.role);
326:         if (opts.note !== undefined) existingEdge.note = opts.note;
327:       } else {
328:         existing.addedBy.push(edge);
329:       }
330:       this.storage.collaborators.put(existing);
331:       return {
332:         profile: existing.profile,
333:         addedBy: existing.addedBy,
334:         role: this.computeEffectiveRoles().get(existing.profile.id) ?? opts.role,
335:       };
336:     }
337: 
338:     let record: CollaboratorRecord = {
339:       profile: opts.profile,
340:       addedBy: [edge],
341:     };
342:     this.storage.collaborators.put(record);
343:     return {
344:       profile: record.profile,
345:       addedBy: record.addedBy,
346:       role: this.computeEffectiveRoles().get(record.profile.id) ?? opts.role,
347:     };
348:   }
349: 
350:   previewRemoveCollaborator(caller: SharingCaller, profileId: string): AffectedCollaborator[] {
351:     let target = this.storage.collaborators.get(profileId);
352:     if (!target) return [];
353: 
354:     let baseline = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
355:     let modified = caller.isOwner
356:         ? this.computeEffectiveRoles({ removedUser: profileId })
357:         : this.computeEffectiveRoles({
358:             removedEdge: { target: profileId, sharer: caller.profileId } });
359: 
360:     return this.#computeAffected(baseline, modified);
361:   }
362: 
363:   /**
364:    * Remove a collaborator by severing the edges that grant them access. This is a *lazy* removal:
365:    * nothing cascades and no records are deleted. The target's record (and crucially, any edges
366:    * where the target is the *sharer* of access to others) is left intact, and dependents who lose
367:    * their only path to the owner simply become unreachable -- they are denied at open() time, not
368:    * pruned here. This makes the removal trivially reversible: re-adding the target (see
369:    * addCollaborator) restores the target and, transitively, everyone they had shared with.
370:    *
371:    *   - The owner severs *all* incoming edges to the target (owner-removal means "gone now").
372:    *   - A non-owner severs only their own `user` edge to the target; if the target retains other
373:    *     edges, they keep access (possibly at a lower role).
374:    *
375:    * `keepUsers` is optional re-root sugar: any listed dependent who would otherwise lose access or
376:    * be downgraded is granted a fresh edge from the caller at their prior role (see
377:    * `#reRootKeptUsers`). Returns the collaborators whose access actually changed (removed or
378:    * downgraded), excluding kept users.
379:    */
380:   removeCollaborator(
381:       caller: SharingCaller, profileId: string, keepUsers: string[]): AffectedCollaborator[] {
382:     let target = this.storage.collaborators.get(profileId);
383:     if (!target) {
384:       throw new Error("User is not a collaborator.");
385:     }
386: 
387:     // Permission check: owner can remove anyone; collaborators can only remove users
388:     // they themselves added.
389:     if (!caller.isOwner) {
390:       let hasEdgeFromCaller = target.addedBy.some(
391:           e => e.type === "user" && e.sharer === caller.profileId);
392:       if (!hasEdgeFromCaller) {
393:         throw new Error("You can only remove users that you added.");
394:       }
395:     }
396: 
397:     let baseline = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
398: 
399:     // Sever the edges that grant the target access. The record is retained even if it becomes
400:     // empty, so the target's own outgoing grants survive and the removal can be undone.
401:     if (caller.isOwner) {
402:       target.addedBy = [];
403:     } else {
404:       target.addedBy = target.addedBy.filter(
405:           e => !(e.type === "user" && e.sharer === caller.profileId));
406:     }
407:     this.storage.collaborators.put(target);
408: 
409:     this.#reRootKeptUsers(caller, baseline, new Set(keepUsers));
410: 
411:     return this.#computeAffected(baseline, this.computeEffectiveRoles());
412:   }
413: 
414:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
415:   // Share link management
416: 
417:   // Enforce that `caller` may manage `link`: the owner can manage any link; a collaborator only
418:   // the links they created. `action` is the user-facing verb (e.g. "revoke", "edit", "copy").
419:   #requireLinkManager(caller: SharingCaller, link: ShareLinkRecord, action: string): void {
420:     if (!caller.isOwner && link.createdBy !== caller.profileId) {
421:       throw new Error(`You can only ${action} share links that you created.`);
422:     }
423:   }
424: 
425:   // Look up a link by id, throwing the caller-facing error if the id is unknown or names an alias..
426:   #requireLink(linkId: string): ShareLinkRecord {
427:     let link = asLink(this.storage.shareKeys.get(linkId));
428:     if (!link) {
429:       throw new Error("Share link not found.");
430:     }
431:     return link;
432:   }
433: 
434:   async createShareLink(
435:       opts: { caller: SharingCaller; role: CollaboratorRole; note?: string })
436:       : Promise<{ key: string; linkId: string }> {
437:     let callerRole = this.#requireCallerRole(opts.caller);
438:     if (roleRank(opts.role) > roleRank(callerRole)) {
439:       throw new Error("You cannot grant a role higher than your own.");
440:     }
441: 
442:     // The link is stored as its first key: the record is keyed by that key's hash.
443:     let { key, hash } = await this.#mintKey();
444:     this.storage.shareKeys.put({
445:       id: hash,
446:       note: opts.note,
447:       created: new Date(),
448:       createdBy: opts.caller.profileId,
449:       role: opts.role,
450:     });
451:     return { key, linkId: hash };
452:   }
453: 
454:   /** Mints another key for an existing link. */
455:   async newShareLinkKey(opts: { caller: SharingCaller; linkId: string }): Promise<{ key: string }> {
456:     let link = this.#requireLink(opts.linkId);
457:     if (link.revoked) {
458:       throw new Error("Share link not found.");
459:     }
460:     this.#requireLinkManager(opts.caller, link, "copy");
461: 
462:     // Re-check the ceiling: the caller's role may have dropped below the link's since it was
463:     // created, and a fresh key must never grant more than the caller currently has.
464:     let callerRole = this.#requireCallerRole(opts.caller);
465:     if (roleRank(link.role ?? "build") > roleRank(callerRole)) {
466:       throw new Error("You cannot grant a role higher than your own.");
467:     }
468: 
469:     let { key, hash } = await this.#mintKey();
470:     this.storage.shareKeys.put({ id: hash, alias: link.id });
471:     return { key };
472:   }
473: 
474:   // Generate a random 128-bit key, returning it along with the hash it is stored under. The caller
475:   // decides whether that hash keys a link or an alias.
476:   async #mintKey(): Promise<{ key: string; hash: string }> {
477:     let rawBytes = new Uint8Array(16);
478:     crypto.getRandomValues(rawBytes);
479:     let key = rawBytes.toHex();
480:     return { key, hash: await hashShareKey(key) };
481:   }
482: 
483:   /**
484:    * Active (non-revoked) share links. The Overseer maps each `createdBy` profile.id to a display
485:    * profile (which may require RPC) to produce `ShareLinkInfo`s; see `getCreatorProfile`.
486:    */
487:   listShareLinkRecords(): ShareLinkRecord[] {
488:     return [...this.#listLinks()].filter(link => !link.revoked);
489:   }
490: 
491:   /**
492:    * Resolve the display profile for a share link's creator using only locally-available data
493:    * (the collaborator table). Returns undefined if the creator is neither a current collaborator
494:    * nor matched here (e.g. the owner), in which case the Overseer resolves it via RPC. The final
495:    * fallback (a bare profile from the id) is also the Overseer's responsibility.
496:    */
497:   getCreatorProfile(createdBy: string): AiChatAuthorInfo | undefined {
498:     return this.storage.collaborators.get(createdBy)?.profile;
499:   }
500: 
501:   updateShareLink(caller: SharingCaller, linkId: string, note?: string): void {
502:     let link = this.#requireLink(linkId);
503:     this.#requireLinkManager(caller, link, "edit");
504: 
505:     link.note = note === undefined ? undefined : note.slice(0, 500);
506:     this.storage.shareKeys.put(link);
507:   }
508: 
509:   previewRevokeShareLink(caller: SharingCaller, linkId: string): AffectedCollaborator[] {
510:     let link = asLink(this.storage.shareKeys.get(linkId));
511:     if (!link) return [];
512:     this.#requireLinkManager(caller, link, "revoke");
513:     if (link.revoked) return [];
514: 
515:     let baseline = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
516:     let modified = this.computeEffectiveRoles({ revokedLinkId: linkId });
517:     return this.#computeAffected(baseline, modified);
518:   }
519: 
520:   /**
521:    * Revoke a share link by soft-revoking it (setting the `revoked` flag) rather than deleting it.
522:    * This is the lazy counterpart to removeCollaborator: the link record and every `shareKey` edge
523:    * referencing it stay intact (no dangling references), but the link contributes nothing to the
524:    * permission graph and its keys can no longer be redeemed. Its copies are deleted outright,
525:    * since no edge ever names an alias. Users who relied solely on it become unreachable and
526:    * are denied at open() time.
527:    *
528:    * `keepUsers` is optional re-root sugar, identical to removeCollaborator. Returns the
529:    * collaborators whose access actually changed (removed or downgraded), excluding kept users.
530:    */
531:   revokeShareLink(
532:       caller: SharingCaller, linkId: string, keepUsers: string[]): AffectedCollaborator[] {
533:     let link = this.#requireLink(linkId);
534:     this.#requireLinkManager(caller, link, "revoke");
535: 
536:     let baseline = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
537: 
538:     link.revoked = true;
539:     this.storage.shareKeys.put(link);
540: 
541:     // Revoking makes the copies useless, and nothing references them, so delete them.
542:     this.storage.shareKeys.byAlias.delete(link.id);
543: 
544:     this.#reRootKeptUsers(caller, baseline, new Set(keepUsers));
545: 
546:     return this.#computeAffected(baseline, this.computeEffectiveRoles());
547:   }
548: 
549:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
550:   // Permission-graph engine
551: 
552:   /**
553:    * Compute the effective role of every collaborator -- the maximum role reachable from the owner
554:    * through valid permission edges. A collaborator absent from the returned map has no access.
555:    *
556:    * The owner is the implicit root at "build". Each edge grants min(edge role, sharer's effective
557:    * role):
558:    *   - A "user" edge's sharer is the owner (effective "build") or another collaborator.
559:    *   - A "shareKey" edge's "sharer" is the key's creator; the edge grants the key's role bounded
560:    *     by the creator's effective role.
561:    *
562:    * Optional modifications model a hypothetical change, used by the preview methods:
563:    *   - `removedUser`: a profileId treated as removed (excluded from the graph entirely).
564:    *   - `removedEdge`: a single user edge (target ← sharer) treated as removed.
565:    *   - `revokedLinkId`: a link treated as revoked (its edges contribute nothing).
566:    */
567:   computeEffectiveRoles(opts: {
568:     removedUser?: string | null;
569:     removedEdge?: { target: string; sharer: string } | null;
570:     revokedLinkId?: string | null;
571:   } = {}): Map<string, CollaboratorRole> {
572:     let removedUser = opts.removedUser ?? null;
573:     let removedEdge = opts.removedEdge ?? null;
574:     let revokedLinkId = opts.revokedLinkId ?? null;
575: 
576:     // Map linkId → {creator, role}, excluding revoked links (the persisted `revoked` flag, and the
577:     // hypothetical `revokedLinkId` used by preview).
578:     let linkInfo = new Map<string, { creator: string; role: CollaboratorRole }>();
579:     for (let link of this.#listLinks()) {
580:       if (link.id === revokedLinkId || link.revoked) continue;
581:       linkInfo.set(link.id, {
582:         creator: link.createdBy,
583:         role: link.role ?? "build",
584:       });
585:     }
586: 
587:     // All collaborators except the removed user.
588:     let allCollabs = new Map<string, CollaboratorRecord>();
589:     for (let record of this.storage.collaborators.list()) {
590:       if (record.profile.id !== removedUser) {
591:         allCollabs.set(record.profile.id, record);
592:       }
593:     }
594: 
595:     // Roles known so far.
596:     let eff = new Map<string, CollaboratorRole>();
597: 
598:     // Effective role of a potential sharer (the owner is the root at "build").
599:     let sharerRole = (id: string): CollaboratorRole | undefined =>
600:         id === this.ownerProfileId ? "build" : eff.get(id);
601: 
602:     // Fixed-point iteration. Roles only increase, so this converges.
603:     let changed = true;
604:     while (changed) {
605:       changed = false;
606:       for (let [id, record] of allCollabs) {
607:         let best: CollaboratorRole | undefined = eff.get(id);
608:         for (let edge of record.addedBy) {
609:           let granted: CollaboratorRole | undefined;
610:           if (edge.type === "shareKey") {
611:             let info = linkInfo.get(edge.keyId);
612:             if (!info) continue;  // link revoked or no longer exists
613:             let creatorRole = sharerRole(info.creator);
614:             if (!creatorRole) continue;
615:             granted = minRole(info.role, creatorRole);
616:           } else {
617:             // Skip the specifically-removed edge.
618:             if (removedEdge && id === removedEdge.target &&
619:                 edge.sharer === removedEdge.sharer) {
620:               continue;
621:             }
622:             if (edge.sharer === removedUser) continue;
623:             let upstream = sharerRole(edge.sharer);
624:             if (!upstream) continue;
625:             granted = minRole(edgeGrantedRole(edge), upstream);
626:           }
627:           if (granted && (!best || roleRank(granted) > roleRank(best))) {
628:             best = granted;
629:           }
630:         }
631:         if (best && best !== eff.get(id)) {
632:           eff.set(id, best);
633:           changed = true;
634:         }
635:       }
636:     }
637: 
638:     return eff;
639:   }
640: 
641:   // The caller's effective role, throwing if the caller has no access at all (which should not
642:   // happen for an authorized session).
643:   #requireCallerRole(caller: SharingCaller): CollaboratorRole {
644:     if (caller.isOwner) return "build";
645:     let role = this.computeEffectiveRoles().get(caller.profileId);
646:     if (!role) {
647:       throw new Error("You do not have permission to share this workspace.");
648:     }
649:     return role;
650:   }
651: 
652:   // Diff two effective-role maps, returning the collaborators whose access changed. A user is
653:   // affected if they had access in `baseline` and either lost it (newRole null) or were downgraded
654:   // (newRole lower than oldRole) in `modified`. Profiles/edges are read from current storage.
655:   #computeAffected(
656:       baseline: Map<string, CollaboratorRole>,
657:       modified: Map<string, CollaboratorRole>): AffectedCollaborator[] {
658:     let result: AffectedCollaborator[] = [];
659:     for (let [id, oldRole] of baseline) {
660:       let newRole = modified.get(id) ?? null;
661:       if (newRole !== null && roleRank(newRole) >= roleRank(oldRole)) {
662:         continue;  // unchanged or (shouldn't happen) upgraded
663:       }
664:       let record = this.storage.collaborators.get(id);
665:       if (!record) continue;
666:       result.push({
667:         profile: record.profile,
668:         addedBy: record.addedBy,
669:         oldRole,
670:         newRole,
671:       });
672:     }
673:     return result;
674:   }
675: 
676:   // Optional re-root sugar for removeCollaborator/revokeShareLink. Must be called *after* the
677:   // edge/key has already been severed in storage. `baseline` is the effective-role map from before
678:   // the severance. For each kept user who would otherwise lose access or be downgraded, append a
679:   // fresh `user` edge from the caller at their prior role (bounded by what the caller can grant),
680:   // so they retain their access independently of the severed path.
681:   #reRootKeptUsers(
682:       caller: SharingCaller, baseline: Map<string, CollaboratorRole>, keepSet: Set<string>): void {
683:     if (keepSet.size === 0) return;
684: 
685:     let callerRole = this.#requireCallerRole(caller);
686:     let afterSever = this.computeEffectiveRoles();
687: 
688:     for (let id of keepSet) {
689:       let prior = baseline.get(id);
690:       if (!prior) continue;  // had no access to begin with -- nothing to keep
691: 
692:       let now = afterSever.get(id);
693:       if (now && roleRank(now) >= roleRank(prior)) continue;  // not dropped -- no edge needed
694: 
695:       let record = this.storage.collaborators.get(id);
696:       if (!record) continue;
697: 
698:       record.addedBy.push({
699:         type: "user",
700:         sharer: caller.profileId,

1: // The workspace git object store.
2: //
3: // Each workspace's Overseer DO holds a real git object database -- SHA-1, zlib-deflated loose
4: // objects, byte-identical to what `git` itself would write -- stored in the `gitObjects`
5: // typed-storage collection. Mainline gadget code is (will be, once the commit-backed code flow
6: // lands) represented as commits in this store, with each GadgetRecord pointing at its head
7: // commit.
8: //
9: // There is deliberately no ref layer: no branches, tags, or HEAD. Our "refs" are the gadget
10: // records, blueprint records, and chats' pinned commits, all managed by the Overseer's own
11: // workflow. Because the store is content-addressed and refless, unrelated histories coexist
12: // freely in the same collection, and related histories (gadgets forked from each other or
13: // instantiated from the same blueprint) deduplicate at the blob/tree level.
14: //
15: // We use real git formats (rather than a git-shaped custom encoding) so that gadget code can
16: // later be exported to and imported from real git repositories, and so agents can eventually
17: // "mount" arbitrary repos through gatekeeper-gated push/pull. isomorphic-git provides the object
18: // codec; we use only its plumbing (writeBlob/writeTree/writeCommit/read*/log), which operates
19: // against a gitdir containing nothing but `objects/**`. The porcelain is off-limits:
20: // `git.commit` requires HEAD/index/config, and `git.merge` cannot represent the merge behavior
21: // we want (see `threeWayMerge`).
22: //
23: // Storage notes:
24: // - Loose objects only, one collection record per object, keyed by oid. isomorphic-git never
25: //   writes deltified data (it only reads deltas in packfiles fetched from remotes), so each
26: //   record is a zlib'd whole object. Dedup comes from content addressing, not deltas.
27: // - No object exceeds ~2MB today (records hold single source files, small trees, and commit
28: //   headers). If large blobs ever appear, chunking records or spilling to R2 is a change local
29: //   to the fs shim below.
30: // - No GC. Dangling objects are only created by accepted merges, imports, and migration -- never
31: //   by in-flight chats -- and are cheap. If GC is ever needed, the roots are enumerable: gadget
32: //   records, blueprint gadget records, live chats' pinned commits, the pin declarations in chat
33: //   logs and compaction checkpoints (closed epochs are reconstructed from them), and the
34: //   `observedCommit` stamps on chats' readFile tool calls (which nothing else roots -- a future
35: //   GC must either root them or the agent's elision path must tolerate a missing commit by
36: //   eliding unconditionally).

43:   writeCommit,
44:   writeTree,
45:   log,
46:   type PromiseFsClient,

56: /**

58:  * `.git/objects/xx/yyyy...`, and `oid` is its 40-hex SHA-1 name. Content-addressed, hence
59:  * immutable and idempotent to rewrite.
60:  */
61: export interface GitObjectRecord {
62:   oid: string;
63:   data: Uint8Array;
64: }

67:  * Typed-storage schema for a git object store collection. Shared between `makeOverseerStorage()`
68:  * and tests so both bind the identical schema.

81: // silently accept writes we didn't intend to store. If we ever need non-object paths (e.g. for
82: // git protocol support), that's a schema extension we design then.

137:       isDirectory(): boolean;

189: /** Options for `GitStore.writeFilesAsCommit()`. */

403: // directory.
404: function buildTreeNode(files: ReadonlyMap<string, string>): TreeNode {
405:   let root: TreeNode = new Map();
406:   for (let [path, content] of files) {
407:     let segments = path.split("/");
408:     let node = root;
409:     for (let [i, segment] of segments.entries()) {
410:       if (segment === "" || segment === "." || segment === "..") {
411:         throw new Error(`invalid file path: ${path}`);
412:       }
413:       let last = i === segments.length - 1;
414:       let existing = node.get(segment);
415:       if (last) {
416:         if (existing !== undefined) throw new Error(`conflicting file paths at: ${path}`);
417:         node.set(segment, content);
418:       } else {
419:         if (existing === undefined) {
420:           existing = new Map();
421:           node.set(segment, existing);

423:           throw new Error(`conflicting file paths at: ${path}`);

437:     if (b.get(name) !== content) return false;
438:   }

442: // =======================================================================================
443: // Three-way merge

445: /** Labels for the three sides of a merge, rendered into conflict markers. */
446: export interface MergeLabels {
447:   base?: string;
448:   ours?: string;
449:   theirs?: string;
450: }

452: /** The result of `threeWayMerge()`. */
453: export interface MergeResult {
454:   /** The merged file map, including any files containing conflict markers. */

457:   /**
458:    * Paths whose merge was not clean, in sorted order. Content conflicts carry inline 3-way

464: /**

466:  * Never throws on conflict -- conflicted files get inline 3-way markers
467:  * (`<<<<<<<`/`|||||||`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>`, diff3 style) and are reported in `conflictPaths`,

469:  *
470:  * This deliberately replaces both Yjs merging (CRDT merge across divergent bases produces
471:  * nonsense) and isomorphic-git's `merge`/`mergeTree` (which throw on both-sides-added conflicts
472:  * before any merge driver runs, and require an index). The common ancestor is always explicitly
473:  * known in our workflow -- the chat's last merged commit -- so no merge-base discovery is
474:  * needed.
475:  *
476:  * Per-file semantics:
477:  * - changed on one side only (including deletion): that side wins;
478:  * - identical change on both sides (including both deleted): clean;
479:  * - deleted on one side, changed on the other: the changed content survives, reported as a
480:  *   conflict;
481:  * - changed on both sides (including both-added): line merged via diff3, conflicting hunks
482:  *   marked.
483:  */

485:     base: ReadonlyMap<string, string>,
486:     ours: ReadonlyMap<string, string>,
487:     theirs: ReadonlyMap<string, string>,
488:     labels: MergeLabels = {}): MergeResult {
489:   let files = new Map<string, string>();

492:   let allPaths = [...new Set([...base.keys(), ...ours.keys(), ...theirs.keys()])].toSorted();

495:     let o = ours.get(path);
496:     let t = theirs.get(path);

498:     if (o === t) {
499:       // Identical on both sides (possibly both deleted, possibly an identical add).
500:       if (o !== undefined) files.set(path, o);

503:       if (t !== undefined) files.set(path, t);

513:       // against an empty base marks the entirety of both sides as conflicting).
514:       let merged = mergeText(b ?? "", o, t, labels);
515:       files.set(path, merged.text);
516:       if (!merged.clean) conflictPaths.push(path);
517:     }
518:   }
519: 
520:   return { files, conflictPaths };
521: }
522: 
523: // A zero-width boundary after every "\n"; split() then keeps each terminator with its line.
524: const LINE_BOUNDARY = /(?<=\n)/;
525: 
526: /**
527:  * Split `text` into lines, each keeping its trailing "\n", so `lines.join("") === text` always
528:  * holds. The consumer -- the diff3 merge below -- reassembles content from the pieces it
529:  * computes over, so the split must be
530:  * lossless above all: only "\n" ends a line, and a bare "\r" (or U+2028/U+2029) stays *inside*
531:  * its line rather than acting as a boundary, which merely makes diffs and merges of such exotic
532:  * line endings coarser -- whereas the obvious `/^.*$/m`-style split treats those characters as
533:  * boundaries it cannot retain, silently corrupting any content that uses them. A boundary
534:  * always follows "\n", so it can never split a UTF-16 surrogate pair.
535:  */
536: export function splitLines(text: string): string[] {
537:   return text === "" ? [] : text.split(LINE_BOUNDARY);
538: }
539: 
540: // A conflict hunk at end-of-file may lack a trailing newline; give it one so the following
541: // marker starts its own line. (isomorphic-git glues the marker onto the last line instead.)
542: function withFinalNewline(text: string): string {
543:   return text === "" || text.endsWith("\n") ? text : `${text}\n`;
544: }
545: 
546: function mergeText(base: string, ours: string, theirs: string, labels: MergeLabels):
547:     { clean: boolean, text: string } {
548:   // diff3 operates on arrays of lines; splitLines keeps each line's terminator, so join("")
549:   // reassembles losslessly. (isomorphic-git's mergeFile splits with a regex that treats bare
550:   // "\r"/U+2028/U+2029 as boundaries it then drops, corrupting content that uses them; ours
551:   // keeps such characters inside their line instead.)
552:   let regions = diff3Merge(
553:       splitLines(ours), splitLines(base), splitLines(theirs));
554: 
555:   let clean = true;
556:   let text = "";
557:   for (let region of regions) {
558:     if ("ok" in region) {
559:       text += region.ok.join("");
560:     } else {
561:       clean = false;
562:       text += `<<<<<<< ${labels.ours ?? "ours"}\n`;
563:       text += withFinalNewline(region.conflict.a.join(""));
564:       text += `||||||| ${labels.base ?? "base"}\n`;
565:       text += withFinalNewline(region.conflict.o.join(""));
566:       text += "=======\n";
567:       text += withFinalNewline(region.conflict.b.join(""));
568:       text += `>>>>>>> ${labels.theirs ?? "theirs"}\n`;
569:     }
570:   }
571:   return { clean, text };
572: }
573:

581:  * convention until users can customize their commit identity.)
582:  */

1: ---
2: name: write-gatekeeper
3: description: Guides implementation of Gatekeeper Workers that bridge Gadgets to external services. Covers auth, capability-based API design, approval queue integration, caching, and action simulation. Load when creating, modifying, or reviewing the implementation of a gatekeeper.
4: ---
5: 
6: # Writing a Gatekeeper
7: 
8: A Gatekeeper is a Cloudflare Worker that mediates all access between a Gadget and an external service. It implements a three-tier hierarchy:
9: 
10: - **Vendor** (`GatekeeperVendor`, a `WorkerEntrypoint`) — top-level entry for the service. One per service.
11: - **User** (`GatekeeperUser`, a `WorkerEntrypoint` with `ctx.props`) — a human user's authenticated connection.
12: - **Instance** (`Gatekeeper<Session>`, a DO facet of the Overseer) — per-resource, per-Gadget binding that provides the Session API.
13: 
14: Read `packages/workshop-shared/src/gatekeeper.ts` for the canonical interfaces and detailed JSDoc.
15: 
16: ## Seven responsibilities
17: 
18: 1. **Auth management** — Manage authorization to the external service via OAuth (or similar), on behalf of the human end user. This means managing "connected accounts" — token storage, refresh, and revocation in a `UserAccount` Durable Object.
19: 
20: 2. **API design** — Provide a TypeScript API wrapper around the service's API, compatible with Cap'n Web RPC. The interface should be designed around capability-based security: object-oriented, with separate interfaces representing logical resources. For example, the Google Docs gatekeeper provides an interface to a *specific* document, rather than a coarse-grained interface where you pass the doc ID to every method. **IMPORTANT:** When writing a new gatekeeper, design a proposed API and then STOP to let the operator review and make changes before proceeding with the rest of the implementation. Getting the API right is the most important and delicate part of creating a new gatekeeper.
21: 
22: 3. **Fine-grained resource granting** — Enable the end user to grant access to agents at fine granularities, in addition to coarse-grained access. For example, a user may want to give an agent access to a specific Google Doc or GitHub repo, rather than granting broad access to everything they can do. This should be straightforward given a capability-based API. That said, broad access should also be allowed when it makes sense. Consider carefully which granularities are meaningful — a Jira gatekeeper might support "whole service", "project", and "issue" granularities, but it would be silly to support granting access to a single field of an issue separately.
23: 
24: 4. **Logging & approvals** — Every action the agent or gadget performs must be logged via the `ApprovalQueue` API. Every action with an externally-visible side effect must be submitted via `submitAction()`, and must not actually be performed until `applyAction()` has been called. Read-only observations must call `authorizeObservation()` before returning data to the caller.
25: 
26: 5. **Caching** — When it makes sense, cache remote content in the gatekeeper's DO storage to improve performance when agents or gadgets repeatedly read the same data. Caching also enables a better TypeScript API when the service's underlying API has an inconvenient data shape. For example, Gmail's API for listing threads returns only thread IDs without metadata, requiring a callback for each thread; with caching, the gatekeeper can provide an API that returns rich thread summaries directly, reading from local content synchronized with Gmail as needed. See Phase 2 for implementation guidance.
27: 
28: 6. **Simulation** — Actions submitted but not yet applied should be simulated as if they already occurred, to the maximum extent reasonable. If the caller reads back data, it should observe the data as if pending actions had been applied, even though they haven't yet. This allows the agent to continue working without waiting for each approval, and allows the end user to batch-approve a lot of work at once. Simulation may leverage caching (updating the cache on submit, clearing or repopulating it on reject), or it may work by storing pending actions separately and adjusting read results at query time — the latter is arguably cleaner but trickier to implement correctly. See Phase 2 for implementation guidance.
29: 
30: 7. **Observer verification** — When a Gadget is shared, collaborators may "observe" data the Gadget previously read through the gatekeeper. The gatekeeper must ensure each collaborator could access that data themselves, via `getVerifier()` / `addObserver()` / `removeObserver()`. The interface methods are mandatory — a gatekeeper won't type-check without them — so include at least minimal versions in Phase 1; but *choosing and implementing the right strategy* is a Phase 2 security concern, like logging/approvals. See [Observer verification](#observer-verification).
31: 
32: ## Phase 1: Core implementation
33: 
34: In the first phase, focus only on responsibilities 1 - 3, though keeping in mind that 4 - 7 will need to be implemented later. Note the observer methods of responsibility 7 (`getVerifier`/`addObserver`/`removeObserver`) are required for the code to type-check, so the skeleton includes minimal versions; you flesh out the actual strategy in Phase 2.
35: 
36: ### Step 1: Understand the external service
37: 
38: Study the service's API docs. Identify:
39: - Auth model (OAuth 2.0, API keys, etc.)
40: - Resources to expose and what access granularities make sense
41: - Which operations are observations (read-only) vs. actions (side effects)
42: 
43: ### Step 2: Design the Session types
44: 
45: Create `src/types.d.ts` defining the Session interface (and Hook interface if the service pushes events — see [Hooks](#hooks-push-notifications)).
46: 
47: Before designing, read `packages/workshop-shared/node_modules/capnweb/README.md` to understand what Cap'n Web RPC supports — this determines what types and patterns are expressible in the Session interface.
48: 
49: Design principles:
50: - One interface per logical resource type, not a god-object
51: - Methods return structured data, not raw API responses
52: - Use capability-based design principles: make it easy to limit authority in useful ways by simply limiting access to specific objects or allowing/blocking specific methods
53: - Simplify API complexities that are not likely to matter to agents and gadgets; design for a more novice user and common use cases
54: - Consider what URL patterns `getGatekeeperClassFor()` should match — each pattern maps to a resource granularity
55: - Include JSDoc comments; these types serve as the agent's API documentation. See [Documenting the API](#documenting-the-api-typesdts) below.
56: 
57: #### Documenting the API (`types.d.ts`)
58: 
59: This JSDoc is the agent's sole documentation for the API, so keep it **narrowly focused on what the agent needs to use each method**: what it does, its parameters, the returned data shape, and any errors the caller must handle.
60: 
61: Do NOT leak details the caller doesn't need to use the API — the approval queue (never mention `submitAction`/`applyAction`/approvals; correct simulation keeps this invisible), or gatekeeper internals (caching, DO storage, OAuth, syncing). Document those in the `.ts` implementation or PR, never in the agent-facing `.d.ts`.
62: 
63: ### Step 3: STOP — Present API for review
64: 
65: **Do not proceed without operator approval.**
66: 
67: Present the proposed `types.d.ts` and explain the design: what resource granularities are supported, what Session methods do, and what trade-offs were made. The API is the most important and delicate part of a gatekeeper — getting it wrong means rebuilding. Wait for the operator to review and approve (or request changes) before continuing.
68: 
69: Also confirm the JSDoc follows [Documenting the API](#documenting-the-api-typesdts) — no approval-queue or implementation details leaked in.
70: 
71: ### Step 4: Implement
72: 
73: See [SKELETON.md](SKELETON.md) for a complete implementation template.
74: 
75: Package structure:
76: ```
77: packages/gatekeeper-<name>/
78: ├── src/
79: │   ├── configurator/         # Optional resource-picker UI modules and UI-facing types
80: │   ├── <name>.ts              # Vendor, UserAccount, UserImpl, GatekeeperImpl, SessionImpl
81: │   ├── types.d.ts             # Session/Hook types (compile-time)
82: │   ├── types.txt -> types.d.ts  # Symlink (runtime, for getTypeScriptTypes())
83: │   └── <name>-api.ts          # (optional) Helper wrapping the service's HTTP API
84: ├── wrangler.jsonc
85: ├── package.json
86: └── tsconfig.json
87: ```
88: 
89: ### Step 5: Configure and register
90: 
91: Add a service binding to `packages/workshop-backend/wrangler.jsonc`:
92: ```jsonc
93: {
94:   "binding": "GATEKEEPER_<NAME>",
95:   "service": "gatekeeper-<name>",
96:   "entrypoint": "GatekeeperVendor"
97: }
98: ```
99: 
100: The backend auto-discovers vendors from `GATEKEEPER_`-prefixed bindings (see `packages/workshop-backend/src/user.ts`).
101: 
102: ### Step 6: Add resource selection UI
103: 
104: Add a resource selection UI for each resource type returned in `getSupportedResources()`. This will be used by users to select the specific resource.
105: 
106: - Workshop calls `GatekeeperUser.startResourceConfigurator(resourceUrlPattern)` with the selected resource's `urlPattern`.
107: - Return `iframeHtml` of the selection UI and `ui` for any RPCs that UI needs.
108: - When the user selects "Add connection", Workshop asks the iframe for the selected resource URL.
109: 
110: Keep the iframe-facing capability narrow, only what's necessary to provide desired interface to help user find and select the resource.
111: 
112: #### Optional helper: `@gadgets/configurator-ui`
113: 
114: For simple configuration UIs, consider using `@gadgets/configurator-ui`. It provides the basic form components that look consistent to the Gadget Workshop and a build script that turns `src/configurator/*-ui.tsx` into `iframeHtml`. Gatekeepers with more specialized UI needs can produce their own `iframeHtml`.
115: 
116: If you use this:
117: 
118: - UI modules live in `src/configurator/*-ui.tsx`.
119: - `resourceUrl()` returns the selected resource URL.
120: - `src/configurator/*-types.d.ts` describes the iframe-facing `ui` API.
121: - `scripts/build-gatekeeper-configurator.ts` generates `src/generated/*.txt`.
122: - Nothing invokes `build-gatekeeper-configurator.ts` by hand. `vite.config.ts` re-exports the
123:   shared `build` and `build:configurator` Vite+ tasks from
124:   `scripts/gatekeeper-configurator-vite-config.ts`; `build` is just `tsc` and depends on
125:   `build:configurator`, which carries `VITE_FRONTEND_ERROR_REPORTING` in its fingerprint, and
126:   `deploy` runs `vp run --no-cache build:configurator && wrangler deploy` — deploys never replay a
127:   cached artifact. There is no `build` script
128:   and no direct builder call, because a script running the builder gets vp's stripped environment
129:   and bakes the wrong flag into the shipped HTML.
130: 
131: ##### Pre-filling the form from a known resource URL
132: 
133: When something already knows the exact resource — most importantly an AI agent's `requestConnection` (which passes a concrete `resourceUrl`) — the configurator should open **pre-filled and editable**, not blank. The runtime handles this for you:
134: 
135: - If your value keys already match the `urlPattern`'s named groups (e.g. pattern `.../area/:areaId` with a value key `areaId`), prefill works automatically — no code needed.
136: - Otherwise, implement the optional `initialValuesFromResourceUrl({ resourceUrl, resourceUrlPattern, ui })` on your spec to map a concrete URL back to your form values. Keep it pure where possible (parse the URL); it may use `ui` and may be async. Example (GitHub, whose value is `repoFullName` but pattern is `:owner/:repo`):
137: 
138:   ```ts
139:   initialValuesFromResourceUrl({ resourceUrl }) {
140:     const [owner, repo] = new URL(resourceUrl).pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean);
141:     return owner && repo ? { repoFullName: `${owner}/${repo}` } : {};
142:   },
143:   ```
144: 
145:   The runtime seeds these values before first render and reflects them in `Autocomplete`/`TextInput`/`RadioCards` inputs. Make sure your `resourceUrl(values)` and `initialValuesFromResourceUrl(url)` are inverses so a prefilled form round-trips to the same URL. **Every gatekeeper with selectable resources should support this** so agents can fully pre-configure a connection.
146: 
147: ### Step 7: STOP — Ask operator whether to proceed to phase 2
148: 
149: The operator may prefer to implement phase 2 later, perhaps in a new context. Stop here and ask the operator whether to proceed.
150: 
151: ## Phase 2: Logging, approvals, caching, simulation, and observers
152: 
153: In this phase, we focus on responsibilities 4-7. These are typically added as a second pass, after the core gatekeeper works. They may be implemented in a separate session.
154: 
155: ### Logging and approvals
156: 
157: Go through all the API methods and decide where to insert calls to the `ApprovalQueue`.
158: 
159: - Any operation which reads external data (but with no side effects) must call authorizeObservation().
160: - Any operation which has visible side effects on the world must call submitAction(), and must not actually apply the action until approved.
161: 
162: Study the `ApprovalQueue` API in `gatekeeper.ts` for details.
163: 
164: It's critically important that you add `ApprovalQueue` to all API operations that interact with the outside world, otherwise the gatekeeper security model is broken.
165: 
166: ### Caching
167: 
168: Store fetched data in the gatekeeper's DO storage (`this.ctx.storage`) to avoid redundant API calls. The cache also enables a better API shape when the service's native data model is awkward — e.g., Gmail's list API returns thread IDs without metadata, but with caching the Session can return richer summaries directly.
169: 
170: - Use TTLs or revision IDs to keep the cache fresh.
171: - Cache transformed data (e.g., Markdown) rather than raw API responses when the transformation is expensive.
172: 
173: PROTIP: The relatively new API `this.ctx.storage.kv` provides synchronous versions of the traditional Durable Object storage API, e.g. `get` and `put`. Use these instead of the old asynchronous methods. (Note that the synchronous API does not provide "batch" versions of `get()` and `put()`, but you don't really need them since simply making multiple calls is efficient.)
174: 
175: PROTIP: `this.ctx.storage.sql` gives you access to a full, private SQLite database. Use this when the full power of SQL is useful, but prefer KV for simple things.
176: 
177: The full Durable Objects storage API (including synchronous KV and SQLite) is documented at: https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/
178: 
179: ### Simulation
180: 
181: When `submitAction()` has been called but `applyAction()` hasn't, reads should reflect the pending action. This allows the calling agent or gadget to be unaware of the approvals mechanism, and proceed with follow-on work immediately. The end user is able to approve a whole batch of changes at once, later on.
182: 
183: Two possible implementation approaches include:
184: 
185: 1. **Mutate the cache** — Apply the action's effects to cached data on submit. On `rejectAction()`, invalidate or rebuild the cache. Simple; works well when the cache is already a transformed view. Don't forget to re-apply any queued actions when updating the cache.
186: 
187: 2. **Overlay at read time** — Store pending actions separately; merge them into read results on demand. Cleaner separation; better when the overlay logic is straightforward.
188: 
189: Choose based on the service's data model and the complexity of simulating each action type.
190: 
191: Keep in mind that the agent calling the API (or the agent writing a gadget to call it) is generally not aware that actions do not take place immediately. If the simulation is correct, the agent doesn't need to be aware. If the simulation has gaps, you may want to mention it in your API's doc comments, so that the calling agent knows to work around them — but ideally there are no gaps and the calling agent does not need to think about it.
192: 
193: For concrete examples, see the Google gatekeeper's Google Docs simulation/cache handling and BigQuery dry-run scope enforcement.
194: 
195: ### Observer verification
196: 
197: This is responsibility 7. When a Gadget is shared, each non-owner collaborator becomes an **observer** of every gatekeeper bound to the Gadget, and may see data the Gadget previously read. The gatekeeper's job is to refuse — or forward-restrict — observers who couldn't access that data themselves.
198: 
199: Three methods implement this (full JSDoc in `gatekeeper.ts`):
200: 
201: - `GatekeeperUser.getVerifier()` — mints a `GatekeeperUserVerifier` (a persistent service stub) representing *this* user's account. The overseer mints one per open and **only ever passes it back to a gatekeeper of the same vendor**, so the gatekeeper may trust whatever it learns from it.
202: - `Gatekeeper.addObserver(id, verifier)` — must **throw** if the user represented by `verifier` is not allowed to observe everything read through this gatekeeper so far. The overseer calls it on **every open by every authorized observer** (re-verification, so revoked access is caught at the next open); cache as needed if the check is expensive. `id` is an opaque, stable per-(user,gadget) string.
203: - `Gatekeeper.removeObserver(id)` — idempotent; drop a tracked observer.
204: 
205: #### The verifier "non-standard method" pattern
206: 
207: `GatekeeperUserVerifier` has no methods of its own — it's an opaque token. To actually answer "can this observer access X?", define a vendor-specific interface that **extends `GatekeeperUserVerifier`** with your own methods, implement it on a `WorkerEntrypoint` that queries the service using the **observer's own token**, and cast the `Fetcher` back to that interface inside `addObserver`. The overseer's same-vendor guarantee is what makes the cast safe.
208: 
209: ```typescript
210: // In types/impl: a verifier interface with non-standard methods.
211: export interface MyVerifierApi extends GatekeeperUserVerifier {
212:   hasResourceAccess(resourceId: string): Promise<boolean>;
213: }
214: 
215: type MyVerifierProps = { userObjectId: string };
216: 
217: export class MyVerifier extends WorkerEntrypoint<Env, MyVerifierProps>
218:     implements MyVerifierApi {
219:   async hasResourceAccess(resourceId: string): Promise<boolean> {
220:     // Query the service with the OBSERVER's own token (this.ctx.props.userObjectId).
221:     try {
222:       await myApiForObserver(this.ctx).getResource(resourceId);
223:       return true;
224:     } catch (error) {
225:       // Distinguish "no access" from "transient failure":
226:       //   - auth/permission/not-found (401/403/404) → false (they can't see it)
227:       //   - anything else → rethrow, so the open fails loudly rather than silently denying
228:       if (isNoAccessStatus(statusOf(error))) return false;
229:       throw error;
230:     }
231:   }
232: }
233: 
234: // In GatekeeperUser:
235: async getVerifier(): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>> {
236:   return this.ctx.exports.MyVerifier({ props: { userObjectId: this.ctx.props.userObjectId } });
237: }
238: ```
239: 
240: `MyVerifier` is a `WorkerEntrypoint`, so it needs **no migration entry**, but (like all entrypoints) it must be `export`ed from the worker's main module so `ctx.exports.MyVerifier(...)` resolves.
241: 
242: #### Choosing a strategy (per resource type / binding)
243: 
244: Strategy is chosen **per `Gatekeeper` DO class / binding**, not per package — one package may use several (e.g. Google: Gmail=A, Doc=B, BigQuery=C).
245: 
246: - **A — Private-only.** `addObserver()` always throws; `removeObserver()` is a no-op. `getVerifier()` must still exist (the overseer mints it) but is never consulted. Use when the resource is too sensitive to share and there is no per-observer access oracle (e.g. a personal Gmail mailbox).
247: - **B — ACL check (single unit).** The binding is one atomic resource; sub-resources inherit its ACL. `addObserver()` calls a verifier method to confirm the observer can access it and throws otherwise; `removeObserver()` is a no-op; nothing is tracked and no `excludeObservers` is ever needed. Use for repo / document / page / team / single-project bindings.
248: - **C — Data-set tracking.** The binding spans sub-resources with **distinct ACLs**, and there is a **per-observer access oracle** for each. The DO logs the data sets actually observed and the current observers; `addObserver()` verifies the observer against **every** logged set (plus a coarse membership baseline) and **stores their verifier**; each later observation that first touches a **new** set re-checks all stored observers and sets `excludeObservers` for any who fail. Use for workspace / organization / dataset-spanning bindings.
249: - **D — Low-stakes.** `addObserver()` / `removeObserver()` are no-ops; `getVerifier()` returns a trivial verifier with a no-op public method such as `verify(): void {}` (an empty `WorkerEntrypoint` is not registered in `ctx.exports`). Use when any collaborator may observe (personal, low-stakes services).
250: 
251: The **B-vs-C decision** (the "broad binding" lens): use C only when **both** (1) the binding spans sub-resources with distinct ACLs *and* (2) there's a per-observer oracle to check each against. If one ACL covers everything → B. If there's no oracle → A or D.
252: 
253: #### Implementing strategy C
254: 
255: Route **every data-revealing observation** through a helper that takes the set id(s) the observation reveals, instead of calling `authorizeObservation()` directly:
256: 
257: ```typescript
258: // On the Gatekeeper DO. `setIds` are the data sets this observation reveals.
259: async authorizeSetObservation(
260:     queue: RpcStub<ApprovalQueue>, setIds: string[], description: ObservationDescription) {
261:   const check = setIds.length > 0
262:       ? await this.#prepareSetObservation(setIds)
263:       : { pendingSets: [], excludeObservers: undefined };
264:   await queue.authorizeObservation({ ...description, excludeObservers: check.excludeObservers });
265:   for (const setId of check.pendingSets) this.#markSetObserved(setId);
266: }
267: 
268: async #prepareSetObservation(setIds: string[]) {
269:   const pendingSets = [...new Set(setIds)].filter(id => !this.#isSetObserved(id));
270:   if (pendingSets.length === 0) return { pendingSets, excludeObservers: undefined };
271:   // This synchronous state change is visible to addObserver() before verifier RPCs can interleave.
272:   for (const setId of pendingSets) this.#markSetPendingIfUnknown(setId);
273:   const excluded = new Set<string>();
274:   for (const [id, verifier] of this.#listObservers()) {
275:     for (const setId of pendingSets) {
276:       if (!(await verifier.hasSetAccess(setId))) { excluded.add(id); break; }
277:     }
278:   }
279:   return {
280:     pendingSets,
281:     excludeObservers: excluded.size > 0 ? [...excluded] : undefined,
282:   };
283: }
284: ```
285: 
286: Key points for C:
287: 
288: - **Use two durable states: pending and observed.** Mark unknown sets pending before the first await, recheck pending sets on every retry, and promote them only after `authorizeObservation()` succeeds. A failed authorization leaves them pending. `addObserver()` must check both states and loop until no unchecked sets remain before synchronously storing the verifier; this also closes admission races in either request ordering.
289: - **The session impls must route through this helper**, not `approvalQueue.authorizeObservation()`. If sessions hold the raw queue (not the DO), thread a small prepare hook/callback into each session and any sub-sessions it spawns, and expose a completion step that promotes its pending sets after authorization. For a single broad binding the hook is active; for the narrow (B) sibling binding it is absent (passthrough). See Linear/Notion for the shared-session-impl case and Supabase for the context-object case.
290: - **One observation may reveal several sets** (e.g. a workspace-wide list whose rows belong to different sub-resources). Pass all of them; union the exclusions over the newly-seen ones. Reads that reveal *no* set (workspace name, member directory, a bare "open") pass an empty list and rely on the membership baseline.
291: - **`addObserver` baseline:** verify the coarse membership (e.g. same org/workspace) that gates the set-independent reads, then verify each already-observed set, then store the verifier. Fail closed if a needed identity is unknown (e.g. an account connected before you began persisting the workspace id → force a reconnect).
292: 
293: #### `excludeObservers` semantics (why conservative is safe)
294: 
295: When `authorizeObservation()` is given `excludeObservers`, the overseer **blocks the observation** if any named observer is still authorized, and only lets it proceed (tearing down the observer) if they've already lost access. So erring toward listing an observer is never a leak — at worst it blocks an observation that could in principle have been allowed. The leak-relevant gate is always the live sharing graph, so stale observer state self-heals on the next open.
296: 
297: ## Hooks (push notifications)
298: 
299: Some services can push events to the Gadget (inbound email, webhooks, chat messages, etc.). A gatekeeper exposes this as a **hook**: the Gadget registers a callback, and the gatekeeper later invokes it when an event arrives. Hooks are persistent — they survive across sessions and server restarts — and are subject to the same observation/action approval model as everything else.
300: 
301: `gatekeeper-email` is the canonical reference implementation. Read it alongside the `HookController`, `HookInitiator`, and `ApprovalQueue.bindHook()` JSDoc in `gatekeeper.ts`.
302: 
303: ### The pieces
304: 
305: - **Hook interface** (in `types.d.ts`): the methods the Gadget implements to receive events, e.g. `EmailHook.receiveEmail(email)`. It is implemented by the Gadget as an **`RpcTarget`** (or a plain function), *not* a `WorkerEntrypoint`. Reference it from `describe()` via `hookTsType`.
306: - **Session method**: a method like `subscribe(callback)` that the Gadget (or, more commonly, an agent in a one-off `executeCode` call) uses to register interest. The `callback` is a **persistent stub** (created by the Gadget with `ctx.restore()`), so it can be stored and re-invoked long after the session ends.
307: - **`HookController`** (a `WorkerEntrypoint` you implement): lets the overseer `enable()` / `disable()` the hook. All the state it needs must live in its `props`, so it is constructed via `this.ctx.exports.MyHookControllerImpl({props})` **at bind time**, immediately before calling `bindHook()` — see below.
308: - **`HookInitiator`** (provided to you by the overseer): you call `startHook()` on it when an event arrives.
309: 
310: ### Lifecycle
311: 
312: 1. **Register.** The Gadget calls your Session method (e.g. `subscribe(callback, filter)`). Inside it, construct a `HookController` whose `props` capture the specifics of *this* registration, then call `approvalQueue.bindHook(controller, callback, description)`. The overseer stores the callback and records the hook (initially **disabled**). Do **not** store the callback yourself — it is bound to the current session and would be revoked when the session ends.
313: 2. **Enable.** When the user approves the hook in the Workshop UI, the overseer calls `controller.enable(initiator, target)`. Store the `initiator` Fetcher somewhere it can be reached when events arrive (e.g. an event-source DO). `target` identifies where the hook delivers (workspace, plus gadget when the hook is pinned to one); persist it alongside the initiator if you display or link to the target — the IDs are fixed when the hook is bound, so there is nothing to refresh. A gatekeeper that doesn't need it still has to declare the parameter, since RPC argument validation rejects arguments the receiver doesn't declare. Avoid storing any other state until enabled; everything else should already be in the controller's `props`.
314: 3. **Deliver.** When the event occurs, call `initiator.startHook()`. This returns `{callback, approvalQueue}` bound to a fresh session. Call `authorizeObservation()` (a hook event is almost always an observation; register actions too if the callback's return value triggers side effects), then invoke the `callback` to deliver the event to the Gadget.
315: 4. **Disable / delete.** The overseer calls `controller.disable()`. Forget the stored `initiator` and clean up all related state — `disable()` may never be called again, though the overseer may later call `enable()` afresh.
316: 
317: Because the callback is a persistent stub tied to a session, the gatekeeper never stores it directly; the overseer hands it back (re-bound to a new session) each time you call `startHook()`. See the SKELETON for the full code shape.
318: 
319: ### Documentation
320: 
321: When defining a session interface with hooks, it's important to include comments that clearly state when a method expects to be passed a *persistent* stub created with `ctx.restore()`, as opposed to a regular RpcStub. The caller needs to do extra work to make sure the stub they provide you is persistent.
322: 
323: ## Tips
324: 
325: - `types.txt` must be a **symlink** to `types.d.ts`, never a copy.
326: - Call `.dup()` on `approvalQueue` stubs before storing in a session, since Cap'n Web automatically disposes all stubs in parameters to an RPC call when the call returns.
327: - `suggestedBindingName` in `describe()` reflects the resource **type** (e.g. `"GMAIL_INBOX"`), not the specific instance.
328: - For read-only or push-only gatekeepers, `applyAction()` / `rejectAction()` / `revertAction()` can simply throw (they'll never be called since the gatekeeper never submits actions).
329: - For `WorkerEntrypoint` and `DurableObject` subclasses, pass credentials and resource IDs via `ctx.props`, not constructor arguments. RPC stubs pointing to these types can be stored in long-term storage and restored later, creating a new instance based on the same `props`.
330: - If the gatekeeper implements multiple unrelated resource types with disjoint APIs, each may have its own `.d.ts` file, so that the `getTypeScriptTypes()` method of the specific `Gatekeeper` implementation only returns the types that matter for it. The `getTypeScriptTypes()` method on the top-level `GatekeeperVendor` should return the concatenation of all of these.
331: - All DO classes must appear in `wrangler.jsonc` under `migrations[].new_sqlite_classes`.
332: - Set a self-destruct alarm in `UserAccount.setCallback()` in case the OAuth flow is never completed.
333: - `authorizeObservation()` may be called *after* fetching data (so the description can include details about what was fetched) but must be awaited *before* returning anything to the caller.
334: - `getVerifier()` / `addObserver()` / `removeObserver()` are **mandatory** — the gatekeeper won't type-check without them. Even a read-only or push-only gatekeeper needs them (sharing is independent of whether the gatekeeper has actions). Pick a strategy per [Observers](#observer-verification): a low-stakes one can be A or D; otherwise B/C.
335: 
336: ## Reference implementations
337: 
338: - `packages/gatekeeper-google/` — OAuth, multiple resource types (Gmail, Google Docs, BigQuery), actions, caching/simulation examples, multiple Session types. **Observers:** all three strategies in one package — Gmail=A (always throw), Doc=B (single-unit ACL via `GoogleVerifier.hasDocAccess`), BigQuery=C (dataset tracking via `hasDatasetAccess`).
339: - `packages/gatekeeper-email/` — Hook-based push notifications, no actions, email address claiming. **Observers:** strategy D (low-stakes no-ops + trivial verifier).
340: - `packages/gatekeeper-github/` — **Observers:** clean strategy B example — `GitHubVerifier.hasRepoAccess` plus a one-method `addObserver`.
341: - `packages/gatekeeper-supabase/` — **Observers:** strategy C with a per-session context object (`authorizeProjectObservation`) — good when sessions already hold a shared context.
342: - `packages/gatekeeper-linear/` & `packages/gatekeeper-notion/` — **Observers:** strategy C where the page/team session impls are shared between the narrow (B) and broad (C) bindings, threading an `observe` hook through sub-sessions; both also handle one observation revealing multiple sets.
343: - `packages/workshop-shared/src/gatekeeper.ts` — Canonical interfaces with detailed JSDoc (`getVerifier`, `addObserver`, `removeObserver`, `GatekeeperUserVerifier`, `ObservationDescription.excludeObservers`).

(End of file - total 343 lines)
